items.bodyEn: Every year from late spring into early summer, dealers drove hundreds of horses to the meadow outside Chiryū for a market that drew buyers from near and far. Hiroshige's print, titled 'Early Summer Horse Market', shows the animals tethered in rows around a great lone pine while traders bargain in its shade. The market gave this station its keeper.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Fifty-three Stations (Hōeidō ed.), Chiryū 'Shuka umaichi'

items.bodyEn: The town is Chiryū, but the Edo-period spelling 池鯉鮒 reads literally 'pond, carp, crucian carp'. The characters are ateji, chosen for their sound and, by the account the Edo gazetteers gave, for the fish kept in the pond of Chiryū Shrine. The plainer spelling 知立, long used for the shrine, is the one on today's maps.
items.sourceNote: Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei (Heibonsha), 池鯉鮒宿; Tōkaidō meisho zue

items.titleEn: An Iris Hidden in a Poem
items.bodyEn: In the ninth episode of the Tales of Ise, the hero reaches Yatsuhashi in Mikawa, in today's Chiryū, where irises bloom beside eight plank bridges. Asked to compose, he begins each line with one syllable of かきつばた, iris: か, き, つ, ば, た. The acrostic device is called 折句, and the poem is attributed to Ariwara no Narihira.
items.ja: {唐衣|からころも} {着|き}つつなれにし つましあれば はるばる{来|き}ぬる {旅|たび}をしぞ{思|おも}ふ
items.kana: からころも きつつなれにし つましあれば はるばるきぬる たびをしぞおもふ
items.sourceNote: Ise Monogatari, episode 9 (Azuma-kudari); Kokin Wakashū, travel poems

items.bodyEn: 次第 began as 'order, sequence', and all three uses keep that sense of one thing following another. After a verb stem it means 'as soon as'. After a noun with だ or で it means 'depends on': it depends on the weather. As the adverb 次第に it means 'gradually'. The first two are formal and common in business.
items.ja: {着|つ}き{次第|しだい}、{連絡|れんらく}します。
items.kana: つきしだい、れんらくします。
